Macworld

Apple has launched an M6 MacBook Pro alongside a new touchscreen MacBook Pro with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. If you’re buying your first MacBook Pro or replacing an older model, now is a good time to consider your options – although we recommend reading independent reviews before committing.

If you already own an M4 or M5 MacBook Pro that meets your needs, there’s little reason to upgrade unless the touchscreen model’s combination of OLED, touch and lower weight appeals to you.

Apple increased MacBook Pro prices by $300 to $500 in June 2026, so discounts and refurbished models remain worth considering. For the best value, compare the non-touch M5 Pro and M5 Max models and any remaining discounted M5 stock with the new models. If your purchase isn’t urgent, it may also be worth holding out for Black Friday deals at the end of November.

The MacBook Pro is best suited to creative professionals, software developers, engineers and other power users who need sustained performance, a premium display, plenty of ports and high memory configurations. If your workload consists mainly of web browsing, office work, studying or light creative tasks, the MacBook Air is likely to offer better value at a much lower price.

In this guide, we’ll help you decide which MacBook Pro is right for you, explain the best times of year to buy, highlight today’s best deals, and consider whether a refurbished model or MacBook Air would be a better choice.

Should you buy a MacBook Pro now?

Now that Apple has announced its latest MacBook Pros, there’s no need to wait for the launch to see your options. The M6 and touchscreen models arrive on November 6. If you’re considering either, we recommend waiting for independent reviews. If you need a laptop immediately, an existing non-touch M5 Pro or M5 Max model could still be a sensible purchase.

Buy a MacBook Pro now if:

  • You’re upgrading from an Intel Mac: Apple is ending support for Intel Macs, so if you haven’t yet switched to Apple Silicon, now is a good time to do so. As Intel Macs reach the end of support, they’ll stop receiving security updates, leaving them vulnerable to newly discovered security flaws.
  • You need a new laptop: If your current Mac is broken, unreliable or slowing you down, there’s little reason to wait.
  • You edit video or create content: Whether you’re editing 4K video, working in Photoshop or Lightroom, producing music or creating 3D graphics, the MacBook Pro delivers the sustained performance creative professionals need.
  • You’re a software developer, engineer or AI professional: Compiling code, running virtual machines, working with AI models or processing large datasets is much faster on the MacBook Pro, particularly the M5 Pro and M5 Max models.
  • You need sustained performance: Unlike the fanless MacBook Air, the MacBook Pro uses active cooling to maintain peak performance during long exports, renders and other demanding workloads.
  • You need professional features: The MacBook Pro offers a Liquid Retina XDR or PROLED XDR display with ProMotion, HDMI, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe charging and higher memory and storage options than the MacBook Air.
  • You find an excellent deal: A discounted MacBook Pro can be a good buy if it meets your needs. Compare its memory, storage, display and processor with the new models before deciding whether the saving is worthwhile.

When shouldn’t you buy a MacBook Pro?

The MacBook Pro is an excellent laptop, but it isn’t the right choice for everyone. If you don’t need its extra performance or professional features, you’ll save money – and probably be just as happy – with a MacBook Air. There are also a few situations where it’s worth waiting rather than buying today.

Don’t buy a MacBook Pro now if:

  • You want a processor upgrade over M5 Pro or M5 Max: The touchscreen models retain the same chip options as their non-touch equivalents. The M6 Pro or M6 Max aren’t expected until 2027.
  • You’re looking for the best price: With new MacBook Pro M6 models now here, discounts on the discontinued MacBook Pro M5 could be more attractive. Black Friday may bring further savings.
  • You mainly use your laptop for everyday tasks: If your workload consists of web browsing, Microsoft Office, streaming, email, video calls or light photo editing, a MacBook Air offers excellent performance for much less money.
  • You’re a student with basic computing needs: If your coursework mainly involves writing essays, researching online or creating presentations, a MacBook Air is likely to be the better value.
  • Portability is your priority: The MacBook Air is thinner, lighter and completely silent thanks to its fanless design, although the touchscreen MacBook Pro is lighter than its non-touchscreen counterpart.
  • You’re on a budget: The MacBook Air delivers outstanding performance for most users while costing significantly less than the MacBook Pro.

For most people, the MacBook Air is the better buy. The MacBook Pro only comes into its own if you regularly run demanding professional workloads that benefit from its active cooling, more powerful chips, superior display, additional ports and higher memory options.

Should I buy a MacBook Pro: At a glance

MacBook Pro: Current line up

Apple’s MacBook Pro range now offers three main choices: the entry-level 14-inch M6, the non-touchscreen M5 Pro and M5 Max models, and the new M5 Pro and M5 Max models with PROLED XDR touchscreen displays. Retailers may also have remaining stock of the previous entry-level M5 MacBook Pro.

MacBook Pro M6

Introduced in October 2026, the 14-inch M6 is the entry-level MacBook Pro. It starts with a 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU, 16GB of unified memory and 1TB of storage. It retains the previous model’s design and non-touch Liquid Retina XDR display, while adding the M6 processor, Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Choose it if you want the Pro’s display, ports and active cooling without paying for an M5 Pro or M5 Max configuration. From $1,999/£1,999.

Launched in March 2026, these models introduced Apple’s Fusion Architecture, combining two 3nm dies into a single system-on-chip. They offer:

  • M5 Pro: up to 18-core CPU (6 super cores, 12 performance cores).
  • M5 Max: up to 40-core GPU, up to 128GB RAM, and up to 8TB storage.
  • Thunderbolt 5, Wi-Fi 7, and Bluetooth 6 via Apple’s N1 wireless chip.

macOS translates taps into clicks for many existing apps; developers can use gesture APIs for more specialised controls.

Reaching 64GB with M5 Pro requires the 20-core GPU; reaching 128GB requires the 40-core M5 Max.

More memory can accommodate larger creative projects, more demanding multitasking and larger local AI models.

Touchscreen MacBook storage: What is the highest capacity?

The entry capacities are unchanged. However, it is possible to upgrade to 16TB on M5 Max, up from 8TB. In order to obtain that capacity buyers need either the 32-core or 40-core GPU.

Apple makes an “up to twice as fast” storage claim that compares a 16TB M5 Max system with an 8TB M4 Max system. We will be running our own benchmarks.

Touchscreen MacBook camera, microphones and speakers

The camera remains a 12MP Center Stage camera with Desk View and 1080p video recording. Advanced video stabilisation is new, however.

Authentication remains Touch ID. Dynamic Island is an interface feature, not confirmation of Face ID or a TrueDepth camera.

Apple retains a six-speaker system, force-cancelling woofers, Spatial Audio and Dolby Atmos support. Apple claims 50% deeper bass and adds closed-lid audio tuning.

The three-microphone array retains directional beamforming, Voice Isolation and Wide Spectrum modes.

Touchscreen MacBook battery

Apple lists video-streaming ratings of 22/20 hours for the 14-inch Pro/Max and 24/22 hours for the 16-inch Pro/Max, the same as the non-touchscreen models.

Touchscreen MacBook Pro connectivity and ports

Both sizes include:

  • One 3.5mm headphone jack with support for high-impedance headphones.
  • Three Thunderbolt 5 USB-C ports, supporting charging and DisplayPort.
  • One HDMI port.
  • One SDXC card slot.
  • MagSafe 3.

Apple quotes Thunderbolt/USB4 support up to 120Gb/s and DisplayPort 2.1.

Apple’s N1 wireless chip, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread are included, but they are not touchscreen-model upgrades.

External display support

The M5 Pro chip supports three external displays at 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz. Alternatively, it can support one 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz or 4K/240Hz display, plus a second at up to 5K/120Hz or 4K/200Hz.

Apple’s PROLED XDR specifications lists 165Hz for the multi-display 4K configurations, rather than the older 144Hz figure.

This or an iPad Pro? Choose the MacBook Pro when desktop Mac applications, its keyboard, ports and professional workflows are essential. Choose an iPad Pro when a handheld tablet and supported Apple Pencil workflow are central. Apple has not established Pencil support, a detachable display or tablet conversion for this MacBook Pro.

Who cares about the iPad mini?

All signs point to a new iPad mini arriving today. (Bear in mind, of course, that signs can be wrong.) Which raises an important question: Who cares?

When it was first unveiled in 2012 the mini seemed like the tablet of the future. Attractive, portable, and capable, it had all the ingredients for success. But since then it’s been squeezed by developments at either end of the range.

iPads have gained bigger screens and more powerful specs at the upper end, and are now suitable for work and entertainment in a way that the diminutive mini can’t match. On the other hand, why buy an iPad mini as well as a phone when you can get a big-screen iPhone such as the 18 Pro Max or Duo and have a capable device that can fulfil both functions? The Duo’s inner screen is 7.6 inches, very nearly as big as that of the original mini and not far behind its current 8.3 inches. And the Duo fits that screen into a far more pocketable chassis.

The iPad mini doesn’t even have affordability to recommend it these days, starting at a scarcely budget-friendly $599. The cheap option is the standard iPad at $449, and that comes with a bigger display.

Today’s challenge will be to make the iPad mini relevant again. An OLED screen is a nice idea, but is it enough to shift perceptions of a product that faces superior alternatives in every direction? What about an IP rating and a 2nm processor? My colleague Mahmoud Itani thinks the iPad mini is ready to become the best tablet for everyone, but it won’t be easy.

All signs point to a new iPad mini arriving today. (Bear in mind, of course, that signs can be wrong.) Which raises an important question: Who cares?

When it was first unveiled in 2012 the mini seemed like the tablet of the future. Attractive, portable, and capable, it had all the ingredients for success. But since then it’s been squeezed by developments at either end of the range.

iPads have gained bigger screens and more powerful specs at the upper end, and are now suitable for work and entertainment in a way that the diminutive mini can’t match. On the other hand, why buy an iPad mini as well as a phone when you can get a big-screen iPhone such as the 18 Pro Max or Duo and have a capable device that can fulfil both functions? The Duo’s inner screen is 7.6 inches, very nearly as big as that of the original mini and not far behind its current 8.3 inches. And the Duo fits that screen into a far more pocketable chassis.

iOS version history: Every iOS and the features it brought

There are significant milestones scattered across the iOS timeline:

Apple

iPhone OS (2007): iOS made its debut in 2007 with the first iPhone. However, when Steve Jobs held the little device aloft revealing it to the world for the first time, it wasn’t running iOS 1. Instead, it was reported by Apple to be powered by OS X, the software for the Mac. Over time it was called iPhone OS, until finally gaining its now legendary name in the fourth generation of the software when it was shortened to iOS in 2010.

iPhone OS 2 (2008): The second major release of the iPhone software was groundbreaking because it brought third party apps and introduced the App Store.

iPhone OS 3 (2009): This update was designed to make it easier to find things, while at the same time adding the ability to have up to 11 pages to the Home Screen. Messages could support MMS, Video recording became possible and it was possible to save voice notes with the Voice Memos app.

iOS 4 (2010): Apple changed the name to iOS and added the ability to put apps in folders for a better organised Home screen with iOS 4. The FaceTime, iBooks and Game Centre apps also arrived. The iPad also joined the scene, sharing the same operating system as the iPhone.

iOS 5 (2011): iOS 5 was introduced along with the iPhone 4S in 2011, which saw the debut of Siri as a built-in part of the operating system. The Notification Centre was introduced and iCloud arrived bringing synchronization between devices. This was the first time iOS could be installed directly on the iPhone without requiring a computer.

iOS 6 (2012): This is where Apple Maps came onto the scene. Podcasts and Passbook (now Wallet) apps also arrived. iCloud Photo Stream made it easier to share photos with family and friends. iOS 6 was the last with a skeuomorphic design.

iOS 7 (2013): With iOS 7 iPhone users got a redesigned user interface, which looked a lot more modern with flatter icons. iOS 7 introduced AirDrop and CarPlay.

Apple

iOS 8 (2014): One of the features of iOS 8 was Continuity, which linked the iPhone, iPad and Mac together, so you could “handoff” tasks from one device to another. Family Sharing also arrived making it easier to manage a child’s iPhone.

iOS 9 (2015): iOS 9 improved the Notes app, added Apple News, and featured a new Night Shift mode that removed some of the blue light that can disturb circadian rhythms and stop someone sleeping.

iOS 10 (2016): There were updates to Messages and changes to the Photos app in iOS 10. A new Home app brought HomeKit control. Maps got a redesign. Universal Clipboard meant that users could copy something on a Mac and paste it on an iPhone, for example.

iOS 11 (2017): Things changed significantly in iOS 11 in 2017 as it brought the first touch and gesture interface, allowing the first iPhone without a Home button – the iPhone X. There was a new Files app making it easier to access content synced or saved in iCloud and the Control Centre got a redesign.

iOS 12 (2018): Screen Time, Memoji, Group FaceTime and Siri Shortcuts were new in iOS 12.

iOS 13 (2019): Another major shift came with iOS 13 in 2019, as Apple’s mobile operating system for the iPad split with the iPhone, with iPadOS powering new iPads. Updates to iOS included Dark Mode, new privacy features and the ability to Sign in with Apple and hide your email address. The Photos and Apple Maps apps got a redesign and a swipe-to-type keyboard was added.

iOS 14 (2020): One of the most notable additions was Back Tap, a feature that effectively turned the back of the iPhone into an extra button. Home Screen widgets and the App Library were also major new features. Starting with iOS 14.2, music recognition was built directly into the operating system via a Shazam button.

October 27, 2016 was a day that shook the laptop market. Some of us are still recovering from what Apple did on that day, and how it lead to insanity amongst devoted Mac users. On that day, Apple introduced the first MacBook Pro with the Touch Bar. And the world was never the same.

Okay, sarcasm aside, the Touch Bar, on the surface, seemed like a good idea at the time. That idea was to provide more dynamic input capabilities than the standard F keys across the top of the keyboard. In our early hands-on of the Touch Bar when it was revealed, Macworld editor Susie Ochs felt like it had potential, despite some lag.

However, the Touch Bar suffered from what seemed like neglect from Apple. Its performance never really improved, and it never evolved beyond those early days. Five years ago, I wrote about how I really tried to like the Touch Bar, but I was ready to move on. I could never adjust my workflow to the accommodate the strip screen, and prefer having physical function keys that I can press without hunting them down with my eyes first.

And now, 10 years after the Touch Bar introduction and almost exactly three years since its discontinuation, Apple will reportedly release a touchscreen MacBook Pro. The Touch Bar was seen by some as an Apple compromise for not having a touchscreen–there was even speculation that the Touch Bar was a precursor to a touchscreen Mac, but Apple shot down that theory. Now, as Apple prepares to launch what most people had given up on, the excitement of those early Touch Bar days can be felt once again.

But I can’t help but wonder if the touchscreen MacBook Pro will follow the same pattern as the Touch Bar: Impressive at first, but as time goes on, it doesn’t seem necessary. According to rumors, Apple will treat touch as an option rather than a necessity, despite attaching a hefty premium to touchscreen devices. macOS Golden Gate is said to be retooled to work with fingers, but Apple will need to be active in touchscreen development to make it more successful than the Touch Bar.

But for now, let’s enjoy the anticipation and promise that Apple’s first touchscreen Mac brings. And pour one out for the Touch Bar that had to die so the touchscreen MacBook could live.
